abstract: Transcription requires RNA polymerase II (Pol II) to disrupt nucleosomes while preserving displaced histones for reuse. How these histones remain available as the polymerase advances is incompletely understood. Here we combine optical trapping and fluorescence imaging to follow Pol II-nucleosome encounters in a simplified mammalian elongation system. Displaced histone particles frequently move with the advancing elongation complex, a behavior termed histone hitchhiking. Phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) reduces nucleosomal blocking and supports histone retention during carriage. Structural predictions suggest that phosphorylated CTD repeats engage basic histone surfaces through variable, charge-complementary contacts. Carried particles can subsequently transfer to upstream DNA, and a broader combination of elongation factors increases upstream transfer. Complexes already carrying a histone particle show increased blocking at a second nucleosome. Other encounters leave one particle on upstream DNA while another moves with the complex, suggesting that transfer of one particle may enable capture and carriage of the next during successive nucleosome traversal. These observations support a model in which reversible contacts with the phosphorylated CTD help Pol II capture and carry histone particles as they dissociate from downstream DNA, keeping them available for upstream transfer and subsequent chaperone-assisted reassembly. Our findings extend the role of the Pol II CTD beyond factor recruitment to histone handling, linking nucleosome traversal to histone preservation.
